Sources indicate that credit for inventing crêpes Suzette is claimed by French restaurateur Henri Charpentier, who in 1894, at age 14, while an assistant waiter, accidentally set a sauce aflame when serving dessert to the Prince of Wales. Once the fire subsided, the sauce was so delicious that the prince asked that the dish be named for a young girl in his entourage, Suzette.

Are Uranus and Neptune Secretly "Rock Giants"? A Noble Gas Might Hold the Answer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps.
  • Scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock.
  • It has been revealed that understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the âice giantsâ, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A latest paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giantâs thick atmospheres.

Scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock. But we canât simply fly a probe out a few billion miles and drill down into their surfaces to determine that for ourselves. Instead, they decided to use proxies, such as the concentration of argon-40, as a rough measurement for how much rock there is below the atmosphere.

It has been revealed that understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas. Or at least, it gives me an excuse to talk about bananas in a planetary science article. Bananas are radioactive, and the thing causing their radioactivity is potassium-40 - a relatively unstable form of a very common element. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Fraser talks about how to plan a mission to Uranus.

Industry observers note that most of this radioactive decay takes place in rocks containing potassium-40, rather than bananas, so one of the most common sources of argon-40 is literally rocks. After it is created, it bubbles up out of those rocks and escapes into its host planetâs atmosphere. In fact, it makes up around 1% of the air youâre breathing right now.

According to recent reports, on the ice giants, this same process could hold - argon-40 could form inside a rocky surface, and then bubble up into the planetâs atmosphere over billions of years. So we should be able to send a probe to measure the concentration of argon-40 in their atmospheres, and that would serve as an effective proxy for the existence of rock under the atmosphere.

Thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. In fact, there was already plenty of it floating around in the protosolar nebula that the Sun and all the planets eventually formed out of. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces.

Fraser talks about efforts to go back to visit the ice giants of the solar system.

Sources indicate that according to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ. This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, thereâs still a lot of debate about where exactly in the solar system the ice giants formed. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. On the other hand, if the theories about them actively moving through the solar system soon after their creation are true, then they would likely have captured a large amount of argon-40, making it useless as an indicator of whether or not the planets have a rocky surface.

Luckily, there is a way to potentially solve this puzzle. Argon-40 has a lighter isotopic cousin, known as argon-36, which is non-radioactive, and doesnât form in decaying rocks. Measuring its level would act like a control group, allowing scientists to estimate how much of the argon present in the atmosphere would have been swallowed at birth, as we have other estimates of the ratio between argon-40 and argon-36 in the early solar system.

It has been revealed that itâs good these sorts of insights are coming out now, as there is right now a mission, Uranus Orbiter and Probe, which is in active development and planned to arrive in the system in the 2040s. That still gives us some time to finalize our theories about what we would expect to find there. And perhaps, once it does arrive, weâll be able to definitively answer whether or not the âIce giantsâ have a truly solid surface or not.

SwRI - SwRI team studies interior composition, origins of ice giants.

O. Mousis et al - Primordial and Radiogenic Argon 40 in Uranus and Neptune.

UT - Argon â The First Noble Gas Molecules Discovered In Space.

Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov.
  • Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.
  • The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Sources indicate that colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Sources indicate that republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Sources indicate that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

According to recent reports, “I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I noted, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of Upcoming Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

According to recent reports, colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” indicates a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

Breaking: The Simons Observatory is Online and Surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background.
  • Sources indicate that we live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods.
  • There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background. Its goal is to detect undeniable evidence of the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. Can this unique survey succeed where others have failed?

Sources indicate that we live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods. While powerful telescopes still perform detailed observations of individual targets, and always will, wide surveys have a power all their own. The ESA's Gaia mission, for example, has completed its survey of billions of stars and generated a massive amount of foundational data that researchers will draw on for decades to come.

There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.

Recent findings suggest that but another Simons Observatory's survey hasn't garnered the same attention that some of the other have. The Simons Observatory (SO) consists of four telescopes working together: three small 0.5 meter aperture 'scopes in its Small Aperture Telescope (SAT) and one large 6-meter one in its Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).

The unusual configuration gives the SO the best chance to observe tiny details in the Universe's first observable light, the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB).

Sources indicate that this image of the Cosmic Microwave Background is from the Simons Observatory, the newest and most powerful observatory to study the CMB. It's unique arrangement of three small and one large telescope increases its resolution by an order of magnitude over its predecessor, the Planck satellite. The Simons Observatory's main goal is to find the elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation, and thereby confirming the Big Bang model of cosmology. Image Credit: Simons Observatory.

The stuff of the Universe was too opaque for light to travel through it at first. Photons were effectively scattered by the hot, dense plasma that permeated the Universe. Eventually conditions changed. The Universe expanded, the plasma cooled, and photons could travel. This was the recombination epoch and it occurred about 380,000 years after the Massive Bang.

Note that the name is historical and reflected our earlier understanding of the Universe. It wasn't actually a recombination, it was the first time that electrons and protons combined to form neutral hydrogen, and that's what made the cosmos transparent. Its name should probably be changed to the combination epoch.

But regardless of its name, the cosmic microwave background is the relic radiation from the Universe's first light, and it holds clues to the Universe, especially to the Significant Bang theory of cosmology.

Recent findings suggest that other efforts have been made to map the CMB. NASA's Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) and the ESA's Planck satellite both made the effort from orbit. Right now, the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and related facilities are doing the same.

The SPT made an key discovery. It detected for the first time what's called the B-mode polarization of the CMB. The B-mode is important because it was created by primordial gravitational waves generated during the epoch of inflation, the first moments of the Universe's inflation. So finding the B-mode was important evidence for the Major Bang theory.

The South Pole Telescope at the AmundsenâScott South Pole Station, Antarctica. The SPT is a 10-meter telescope that is credited with the first detection of the Cosmic Microwave Background's B-mode polarization. Image Credit: By Amble - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/9057466.

Industry observers note that but there was a problem. Gravitational lensing can also create B-mode polarization, and it has nothing to do with the Significant Bang or inflation. It's difficult to tell which source created the B-mode polarization the SPT detected. So its initial detection was put in doubt.

In a recent development, this is where the Simons Observatory comes into the picture. It's been calibrating its instruments for two years and is now getting down to business.

âTo have all the observatory motors humming, gears turning and data flowing makes me joyful, but even more exciting is the prospect of what we could find in its big new deep and detailed maps,â says Simons Observatory Co-Director Suzanne Staggs of Princeton University.

This time-lapse highlights the Simons Observatory's Large Area Telescope scanning the sky in August 2026. Credit: David Boettger.

According to recent reports, the observatory's four telescopes collectively have tens of thousands of microwave detectors, almost 98,000 of them. That's 16 times more than one of its predecessors, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. They're not only mapping the CMB the same way that WMAP and the Planck satellite did. They're also searching for the tiny fluctuations in the CMB, the B-mode polarizations that can confirm the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. If detected, the SO can determine if these are true artifacts of primordial gravitational waves, or artifacts of the polluting gravitational lensing that confounded the SPT.

It'll take years of observations before that can be achieved, but the SO's first observations are already showing the observatory's power. Its sensitivity is meant to be an order of magnitude highter than its predecessor, the Planck satellite. âThe images that weâve made with just a few months of data are already deeper and less noisy than Planckâs, which were collected over years,â notes Simons Observatory Spokesperson Jo Dunkley of Princeton University. That's significant, because the Planck outperformed its predecessor, WMAP, and is considered the benchmark for CMB observations. So the SO is already establishing a latest benchmark for observations.

The SO's unique four telescope design is already showing its value. The large, 6-meter telescope is able to observe more of the sky in higher resolution than other CMB telescopes. Every couple of days, it scans half of the available sky.

âIt is incredibly satisfying to see the early maps, knowing that our initial data places us at the forefront of the field â and that we are poised to go much further,â states Jeffrey McMahon, observatory testing lead at the University of Chicago.

Industry observers note that the SO isn't isolated and alone in its work. All of these CMB surveys and observatories will work together in the end. For example, the SPT and other facilities at its site are mapping gravitational lenses that can interfere with the detection of B-modes from primordial gravitational waves in the epoch of inflation. Those templates can be used to help remove their pollution from CMB surveys. So it's all hands on deck.

This cut-away schematic highlights the Large Area Telescope's Receiver with one of its optical tubes highlighted. Note the pulse tube coolers and the dilution refrigerator. They keep the telescope at the cryogenic temperatures necessary for microwave observations. Image Credit: Simons Observatory/Nicholas Galitzki et al. 2018. Conference Proceedings.

Recent findings suggest that the SO is an observer of polarized light, and that means that while its primary goal is searching for B-mode polarization, its maps have other things to reveal, too. âThere are a number of large surveys adding to our understanding of the universe,â Staggs says. âOur idea is that we can combine our data with theirs to further our discoveries.â.

This is especially true of other wide surveys like the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The pair will create a potent combination for detecting transients across multiple wavelengths. âThe instrument is now sensitive enough that we can see small changes in transients in only a few days, whereas ACT took months,â Devlin claims. âThis enables us to observe entirely newly introduced classes of objects.â Its science observations have barely begun, and it's already giant stellar flares and asteroids in the Milky Way, and activity around a supermassive black holes outside of our galaxy.

But detecting that elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation is the SO's holy grail, and if it finds it, it will be a collective finding in the mass data the observatory will produce. Like other survey telescopes, the data will be released in large sequential data releases.

âWeâll be providing everything to the community through a data management tool, which we hope to have completed for the first data release,â Devlin says.

The initial success of its first science operations is a hopeful indication that it can finally find the evidence of cosmic inflation, the B-mode polarization from primordial gravitational waves in the CMB.

In a recent development, âEssentially, right out of the box, just turning on the instrument, weâre making beautiful crisp images of the Milky Way,â Staggs indicates. Those images are uncovering upcoming observations of the galaxy's magnetic fields, and understanding them is critical to understanding star formation and how the galaxy evolves.

âThis moment marks a major milestone in our effort to understand these big questions about the universe,â Devlin claims. âI think thereâs going to be so many scientific discoveries coming out in the next few years, itâll be hard to keep up.â.

The SO's performance will improve when another three small telescopes are added in 2027. That will also double the Small Area Telescope's number of individual detectors to 48,160 detectors. The original five-year survey has been extended, too.

"Combined with a planned extension of the survey duration to 2035, this expansion will significantly enhance SO's search for a B-mode signal in the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, a potential signature of gravitational waves produced in the very early Universe," explain the authors of a 2026 paper in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

#31544. BA's Best Lasagna

BA's Best Lasagna

📅 07 Feb 2018 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1426 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it.
  • The secret weapon is the meat sauce.
  • Recent findings suggest that one step you can skip: boiling the noodles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it. Layers of slow-cooked pork-and-beef ragù, silky Parmesan béchamel, and pasta bake into a rich, creamy lasagna Bolognese with a browned top and crisp edges. Make the sauces ahead to break up the work, or settle in for a day of very good kitchen smells.

The secret weapon is the meat sauce. Why make meatballs only to break them apart? Searing the meat in large balls leaves room for moisture to escape, so you get deep browning instead of a potful of steam. After a long, gentle braise, a potato masher turns them into ragù. Whole canned tomatoes, crushed by hand, give you control over the sauce’s chunky texture.

Recent findings suggest that one step you can skip: boiling the noodles. In side-by-side retests, regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil!) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. The ragù and béchamel provide enough moisture to cook the pasta in the oven—as long as every noodle is covered. Spread the sauces to the edges, leaving no dry patches, and making sure the sauce totally covers the top layer of noodles before baking. Round it out with homemade garlic bread and a Caesar salad.

Do I need to buy no-boil lasagna noodles?

No—use regular dried lasagna noodles, preferably De Cecco. Skipping the boiling step isn’t the same as using noodles labeled “no-boil.” In our original tests, those absorbed too much sauce, leaving the finished lasagna drier than we wanted.

De Cecco Lasagne No.1 Pasta, 16-oz.

Why doesn’t this lasagna have ricotta or mozzarella?

This is a lasagna Bolognese, built around meat ragù and Parmesan-enriched béchamel rather than a separate cheese filling. The béchamel supplies the creaminess, while Parmesan brings salty, nutty flavor. For a less involved version with a cheese filling, try our Cottage Cheese Lasagna.

What’s the best way to split up the work?

Make the ragù one day, then tackle the béchamel, assembly, and baking the next. For an even lighter second day, make both sauces ahead and refrigerate them separately; rewarm the béchamel just enough to loosen it before layering. The ragù can be refrigerated for up to 4 days or frozen for up to 3 months, while the béchamel can be refrigerated for 1 day.

Watch Chris make BA’s Best Lasagna.

Sources indicate that save recipes and initiative every week with confidence. Download the app.

In a recent development, saving this cooking project for another day? We tasted nine brands to find the best frozen lasagna.

Preheat oven to 225°. Mix 2 lb. ground pork and 1 lb. ground beef chuck (20% fat) with your hands in a large bowl; season generously with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, then mix again. Form into about 18 large meatballs (they don’t need to be perfect—you’ll be mashing them later).

Warm 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in 2 batches, cook meatballs, turning occasionally and reducing heat if bottom of pot looks in danger of scorching, until browned all over, about 6 minutes per batch. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet as they’re done.

Reduce heat to medium. Add 2 oz. pancetta (Italian bacon) or slab bacon, chopped, to pot and cook, stirring often, until lightly browned and beginning to crisp, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, 1 celery stalk, finely chopped, 1 medium carrot, peeled, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until paste is darkened in color, about 2 minutes.

Add ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until almost completely evaporated, about 5 minutes. Add one 28-oz. can whole peeled tomatoes, crushing with your hands, and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring occasionally, until liquid is jammy and reduced by about half, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth and 1 cup whole milk, then return meatballs to pot. Bring to a simmer. Cover pot partially with a lid, transfer to oven, and cook, checking every hour or so to ensure liquid is at a low simmer and adjusting oven temperature as needed, until meatballs are falling-apart tender, 3–4 hours.

According to recent reports, using a potato masher, break meatballs apart and incorporate into liquid (you should have about 8 cups ragù; transfer pot to stovetop and simmer gently to reduce if needed). Taste and season with more salt and black pepper if needed.

According to recent reports, do ahead: Ragù can be made 4 days ahead. Let cool; cover and chill, or freeze up to 3 months.

Industry observers note that melt 7 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in ¼ cup plus 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until mixture smells slightly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisking constantly, add 6 cups whole milk. Increase heat to medium-high and continue whisking until mixture comes to a simmer. Reduce heat to maintain a simmer and cook, whisking occasionally, until béchamel thickens, about 4 minutes. Continue cooking, whisking occasionally and adjusting heat as needed to maintain a gentle simmer, until béchamel is smooth and velvety, 8–10 minutes more. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 oz. Parmesan cheese, coarsely grated (about 1 cup), a pinch of cayenne pepper, and a pinch of ground nutmeg. (You should have about 6 cups béchamel.) Season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Transfer to a large bowl and press plastic wrap directly onto surface; let cool slightly.

Note: You can skip the following boiling step (and save yourself a pot to wash!). In side-by-side retests, the BA Test Kitchen found that regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. To use them uncooked, spread the ragù and béchamel all the way to the edges, covering every noodle completely, and make sure the sauce blankets the top layer of noodles before baking.

Recent findings suggest that if parboiling: Cook 1¼ lb. dried lasagna noodles in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally and separating them so they don’t stick together, until just starting to soften but still snap in half rather than bend when folded; 3 minutes is the magic number. The noodles will be so firm it will just seem all wrong. Using tongs, transfer noodles to a large bowl of cold water to cool. Drain and lay flat in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet, separated by parchment or wax paper.

Lightly coat a 13x9", 4–6-qt. glass or ceramic baking dish with extra-virgin olive oil. Spread 1½ cups ragù in dish. Lay a single layer of noodles over ragù (cut or break noodles as needed to fill any gaps). Spoon 1¼ cups béchamel over noodles, spreading in an even layer with a small offset spatula. Top béchamel with 1½ cups of meat sauce. Repeat layering noodles, béchamel, and ragù 3 more times. Top with a fifth layer of noodles and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Note: For more pasta in every bite, build six layers instead of five. Start with the same 1½ cups ragù on the bottom of the dish, but use 1 cup béchamel and 1¼ cups ragù between the pasta layers. Finish with a sixth layer of pasta and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Cover with a lightly oiled piece of aluminum foil and set lasagna pan on a rimmed baking sheet (just to catch drips). Bake lasagna until bubbling gently around the edges, about 1 hour. Remove from oven. Increase oven temperature to 425° and carefully place rack in top of oven. Remove foil from lasagna and continue to bake until top is browned and crisp around the edges, 10–15 minutes longer. Let sit 10 minutes before serving.

Do ahead: Béchamel can be made 1 day ahead; keep chilled. Rewarm just enough to loosen before using. Lasagna can be assembled 1 month ahead; let cool, then cover with plastic and freeze. Let frozen lasagna thaw overnight in fridge before baking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood. However, scientists have long known that the planets of the Solar System are subject to activity in nearby star systems, including supernovae and other energetic astrophysical events. For example, it is established that intermediate elements and the heaviest elements on the periodic table are created when stars reach the end of their life cycle and explode, sending their outer layers (with these elements) into space.

These include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium. At the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), Prof. Anton Wallner and his team have released the SUPREME project to uncover traces of these elements. Their goal is to use them to reconstruct the history of cosmic events in our neighborhood and shed light on how the heaviest elements are created in nature.

The project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program. Prof. Wallner and his team were one of 319 leading research groups across Europe selected for funding totaling â¬838 million ($918.86 million USD) to pursue projects that could lead to major scientific breakthroughs. The SUPREME project aims to address two fundamental questions in modern astrophysics, focusing on the past 500 million years.

Recent findings suggest that first, there's the question of how nearby supernovae have affected Earth and biological evolution since the Cambrian Period (ca. 538.8 to 485 million years ago), the geological era that coincided with the rapid explosion of complex marine life (aka. the Cambrian Explosion). When the Cambrian began, the continents were largely located in the southern hemisphere and were mostly barren. But as the period progressed and gave way to subsequent geological eras, life began to emerge from the oceans, giving rise to plants, mammals, dinosaurs, and eventually primates.

Recent findings suggest that supernovae, when they happen in our cosmic neighborhood, distribute heavy elements like gold, platinum, lead, and zinc to Earth. Credit: NASA.

Second, there's the question of how the heaviest elements in the Universe are created and distributed; in this case, to the Earth and Moon. To answer these questions, researchers at the SUPREME project will search for extremely rare radioactive isotopes in lunar samples provided by NASA, deep-sea sediments, ice cores, and other geological archives. These archives preserve the history of interstellar material that arrived on Earth over eons, allowing scientists to identify and date nearby supernovae and other nearby energetic events.

Sources indicate that their work will build on the first detection of radioactive isotopes created by a rapid neutron-capture (r-process) event in history, the process by which about half of all atoms heavier than iron are created in the Universe. This occured in June 2026, when scientists from the HZDR made the first significant measurement of curium-247 and plutonium-244 in interstellar matter trapped on Earth. As Prof. Sebastian M. Schmidt, the Scientific Director of HZDR who led the discovery team, remarked in an HZDR statement:.

This award is a remarkable recognition of Anton Wallner's internationally leading research. SUPREME addresses fundamental questions about the origin of the elements and the history of our cosmic environment while building on measurement capabilities that are unique worldwide. We are proud that this pioneering work is being carried out at HZDR.

According to recent reports, to detect and measure rare radioactive isotopes, the researchers will use HAMSTER (Helmholtz Accelerator Mass Spectrometer Tracing Environmental Radionuclides), a new state-of-the-art accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) facility developed by Wallner and his team and installed at HZDR in 2025. Combined with an innovative laser-based technology that dramatically reduces measurement background, the team will be able to detect individual atoms with unprecedented sensitivity, opening new possibilities for astrophysics and other scientific applications.

The results of this project are expected to provide unprecedented insights into the history of our cosmic neighborhood and its possible influence on Earth's geology and species evolution. "Securing one of the European Union's most competitive research grants is an outstanding accomplishment," said Saxony's Minister of Science, Sebastian Gemkow. "This distinction is not only a major milestone in the recipients' scientific careers, but also a significant gain for Saxony as a leading research and innovation hub.".

Industry observers note that “Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his upcoming White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”.

Kaine noted congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

Industry observers note that getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that in the 17th century, King Frederik III of Denmark had a throne made entirely from unicorn horns.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists are uncovering the secrets of narwhal tusks, revealing an unusual internal structure and fresh possibilities for studying decades of environmental change in the Arctic.

Industry observers note that in the 17th century, King Frederik III of Denmark had a throne made entirely from unicorn horns. The extraordinary royal treasure came from an expedition he sent to Greenland, where the king knew the precious horns could be traced to a very real animal. It lived in Arctic waters, had fins instead of hooves, and was known as the narwhal. The expedition was a success, bringing the Danish ruler a throne that became a symbol of prestige and power across Europe. Yet the legendary horn was not a horn at all. It was a tooth.

According to recent reports, and what a peculiar tooth it is. Unlike the curved tusks of elephants and walruses or the incisors of beavers, the male narwhal’s tusk grows forward in an elegant spiral. Usually, it is the left upper canine that extends through the upper lip, twisting counterclockwise as it reaches lengths of up to two meters (6.6 feet), sometimes half the animal’s body length.

Sources indicate that that unusual shape has fascinated scientists for years. Now, an international research team has uncovered something remarkable inside the tusk. Its microscopic building blocks form two intertwined spirals that twist in opposite directions, creating a structure that helps the enormous tooth withstand mechanical stress. The findings, published in Nature Communications, offer a upcoming explanation for the anatomy behind one of nature’s most recognizable features.

According to recent reports, for all their fame, narwhal tusks still hold plenty of mysteries. Scientists do not know exactly how the animals use them, although evidence suggests they play an notable role in mate selection and social interaction. Narwhals have occasionally been observed engaging in playful tusk duels, further supporting a possible connection to reproduction and social behavior. The tusks also continue growing throughout the animal’s life and can themselves reach 70 years of age.

According to recent reports, understanding how such a long, spiraling tooth remains strong requires looking far beneath its surface. “Like bones or other teeth in the animal kingdom, the narwhal tusk is a complex composite material whose structure extends from tiny nanoscale building blocks to the visible form of the entire tooth,” indicates Marianne Liebi, a researcher at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) and co-author of the study.

Most of the tusk consists of dentine, the same material that forms the core of human teeth. A thinner outer layer called cementum covers it, although in most other mammals, this tissue is normally found only around the tooth’s root. Both materials contain collagen fibers reinforced with tiny mineral crystals, combining flexibility with hardness.

The arrangement works somewhat like reinforced concrete. In buildings, concrete withstands compression while a steel framework provides strength against pulling forces. In the narwhal’s tooth, collagen fibers serve as internal reinforcement, while mineral crystals provide hardness. “The narwhal tusk, too, must be both hard and flexible,” Liebi explains. “Only then can it withstand the strong hydrodynamic forces that swimming generates.”.

The challenge for the researchers was finding out how these microscopic materials relate to the enormous spiral visible from the outside.

“The collagen fibers and mineral crystals are on the nanometer scale, while the spiral of the tooth only becomes visible at centimeter and meter lengths,” Liebi explains.

To connect these vastly different scales, the team turned to a specialized X-ray technique called tensor tomography. Unlike an ordinary dental X-ray, which produces an image based on how strongly tissues absorb radiation, this method uses patterns created when powerful X-rays scatter from regularly arranged structures inside a material.

“From these patterns, we can calculate how the nanometer-sized mineralized collagen fibers inside the material are oriented,” explains first author Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo, who joined the project as a PhD student at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and later continued the research as a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark.

The researchers conducted their investigations at three major European synchrotron facilities: the Swiss Light Source SLS at PSI in Villigen, Switzerland, the MAX IV Laboratory in Lund, Sweden, and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in Grenoble, France. These facilities produce the powerful X-rays needed to examine extremely small structures.

During tensor tomography, the tooth is rotated within the X-ray beam and scanned point by point. Millions of measurements are then combined to reconstruct a three-dimensional picture of its internal architecture, connecting the orientation of nanoscale fibers with the structure of the entire tooth.

In a recent development, after collecting this enormous amount of data, however, the scientists encountered an unexpected problem. The spiral they were searching for appeared to be missing.

Industry observers note that “That puzzled us quite a bit,” Liebi recalls. Earlier mechanical tests had suggested that the tusk’s distinctive shape should already be reflected in the arrangement of its collagen fibers and mineral crystals. “But instead of a helix, all we saw was a regular pattern.”.

Sources indicate that the answer emerged when the researchers changed how they examined the data. Rather than concentrating on individual points within the three-dimensional images, they began comparing how those points were oriented relative to one another.

Industry observers note that “When we compared how these points were oriented relative to each other, a directional trend began to appear,” recalls Rodriguez-Palomo. “All we had to do then was connect the dots – as in a children’s paint-by-numbers kit – and suddenly the structure became visible: two intertwined spirals.”.

According to recent reports, the outer cementum layer followed a left-handed helix, while the mineralized collagen structures within the dentine twisted in the opposite direction. Together, these interlocking spirals create an unusually stable architecture, much like the twisted strands of a rope. Their opposing orientations help the tooth resist twisting forces and other mechanical stresses while contributing to its distinctive external spiral.

The researchers are also interested in another remarkable property of narwhal tusks: their ability to preserve a record of the Arctic environment.

Recent findings suggest that led by Henrik Birkedal of Aarhus University in Denmark, the international team is investigating how tusk growth relates to environmental and climate conditions. Much like the annual rings of a tree, the growth structures within a narwhal’s tooth can provide clues about past conditions, including changes in climate and food availability.

According to recent reports, because the tusk grows continuously, it can preserve environmental information across much of an animal’s life, which can approach a century. A tooth once mistaken for evidence of a mythical creature may therefore also hold a decades-long record of life in the Arctic.

DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75689-z.

  • The outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month.
  • According to recent reports, opposition occurs on November 25th.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why late November 2026 is prime Uranus observing season.

The outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month. First, Saturn crossed this mark last month on October 4th, then Neptune followed suit on September 26th. Now, the planet Uranus makes the transition, crossing opposition next week.

According to recent reports, opposition occurs on November 25th. On âU.S. Thanksgiving-eve.â We say âoppositionâ for an outer planet, as a point at which it seems to rise âoppositeâ to the setting Sun as seen from our Earthly vantage point. Orbiting the Sun at a leisurely pace once every 84 years, Uranus has a synodic period of 370 days, meaning oppositions for the planet only slide forward about five days each year. This year sees Uranus reach opposition in the astronomical constellation of Taurus, between the Hyades and the Pleiades open star clusters.

Uranus at opposition for 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

Shout out to the Full November Beaver Moon nearby on the same date as opposition 2026, fresh off of occulting the Pleiades for the Arctic on November 24th.

It has been revealed that uranus reached aphelion 20 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun in 2009, and is now inbound toward perihelion 18.3 AU distant in 2050. In 2033, Uranus will pass the point in Taurus where it was discovered by Sir William Herschel on March 13th, 1781, between the horns of the Bull very near the constellation's border with Gemini. Uranus made spurious appearances on star charts of the era at least 20 times prior to discovery.

The discovery position of Uranus. Credit: Dave Dickinson/Starry Night.

Uranus reached its southernmost point in the sky in 2007, and crossed the celestial equator multiple times from 2011-2012. Uranus crosses the ecliptic plane northward in 2029. Uranus reaches its northernmost in 2032, and then begins the long trek southward. The Moon wonât resume occulting the planet Uranus again until a cycle starting on September 29th, 2029.

Sources indicate that the Moon occults the Pleiades on November 24th. Credit: Occult 4.2.

According to recent reports, observing +5.5 magnitude Uranus is as easy as sweeping the suspect field at low power, and looking for a blue-green âstarâ that obstinately refuses to snap into focus. To my eye, Uranus looks like a tiny planetary nebula or perhaps a distant fuzzy comet. In fact, thatâs exactly what Herschel thought heâd first discovered, back on that fortuitous night in 1781. He later correctly realized after following the upcoming object for several nights that it was a distant, and therefore intrinsically large object far out in the solar system beyond Saturn, then thought to mark its outer boundary. All of this happened in his backyard garden in Bath, England. We can, however, be thankful that the name âGeorgeâ that Herschel proposed to honor his benefactor King George the III didnât stick (!).

One of Herschel's speculum metal mirrors and telescopes at the London Science Museum. Credit: Dave Dickinson.

Sources indicate that can you see Uranus with the naked eye? Topping +6th magnitude near opposition, itâs knocking on naked eye visibility from a good dark sky site. At the eyepiece, Uranus only shows a 4â disk at around opposition, barely resolvable with a telescope and tough to tease out detail.

A fine capture of Uranus from 2017. Credit: Szabolcs Nagy.

Uranus is tipped over 98 degrees (prograde) on its side, the result of some ancient encounter with another large body early in the solar systemâs history. Currently, weâre staring nearly directly at the rotational (north?) pole/hemisphere of the planet, which will be pointed nearly directly towards us in late 2029.

Challenge: Catching the Uranian Moons.

Though Uranus has 29 known moons, only five are within potential reach of amateur telescopes, with +13.9 magnitude Titania being the brightest. Orbiting Uranus once every 8.7 days, Titania reaches a greatest elongation of 28â from Uranus. We once saw a sharp view of the moons observing through the Steward Observatoryâs Kuiper Telescope in the Santa Catalina Mountains outside of Tucson, Arizona. They were a surprisingly easy catch through the enormous 61â telescope.

A fine capture of Uranus and its moons. Credit: Ralph Smyth.

A planetarium program such as Stellarium and Starry Night will show you the current orientation of the moons of Uranus, to help parse them out from any nearby background stars.

In a recent development, the orbits an orientations of the major Uranian moons. Credit: Starry Night.

Recent findings suggest that the orbits of the moons are at the moment nearly perpendicular to our view in 2026, though theyâre edge-on and can transit Uranus as seen from our view once every 42 years. This last occurred on 2006-2009, and will happen again starting around 2048.

Industry observers note that hubble captures a shadow transit of Ariel in 2006. Credit: NASA/ESA/L. Sromovsky/University of Wisconsin.

Will we return to Uranus in the coming years? To date, only one mission has seen the planet close up: NASAâs Voyager 2, which flew past Uranus and its moons in 1986. Cassini-style orbiters have been proposed, though such a mission would be a lengthy affair, needing to first make the trip to the distant ice giant then slow down to enter orbit. As it stands, such a mission would be feasible for around the 2040s time frame.

JWST's view of Uranus and its rings. Credit: NASA/JWST.

Industry observers note that certainly, Uranus calls out for a dedicated mission. But you can explore the planet yourself tonight as it nears opposition for 2026.

#31536. Latest Update: Scientists Just Challenged a Decades-Old Belief About How Cells Work

Latest Update: Scientists Just Challenged a Decades-Old Belief About How Cells Work

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tools scientists use to study cells may be changing the very proteins they observe, raising questions about decades of research into how cells maintain their structure.
  • For decades, textbooks and hundreds of scientific papers have described coronin proteins as important organizers of the internal framework that gives cells their shape and helps them move.
  • In a recent development, coronins are found in organisms ranging from single-celled amoebae to humans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tools scientists use to study cells may be changing the very proteins they observe, raising questions about decades of research into how cells maintain their structure.

For decades, textbooks and hundreds of scientific papers have described coronin proteins as important organizers of the internal framework that gives cells their shape and helps them move. Now, researchers at the University of Basel in Switzerland are revisiting that longstanding explanation, showing how scientific progress can sometimes begin by questioning what we thought we already knew.

In a recent development, coronins are found in organisms ranging from single-celled amoebae to humans. They are involved in essential processes such as immunity, development, and cell survival. Scientists have traditionally viewed them as proteins that interact with actin, a major component of the cytoskeleton. This network of tiny filaments supports a cell’s structure, allows it to move, and helps organize its contents.

A newly introduced study published in PLOS Biology, led by Professor Jean Pieters at the University of Basel’s Biozentrum, challenges that understanding. Using a broad range of experiments to examine coronins in their natural state, the researchers found that these proteins are largely unnecessary for the overall organization of the actin cytoskeleton.

In a recent development, “Over the years, my laboratory failed to find evidence for a direct role of coronin proteins in actin binding and modulation across a wide range of model systems,” notes Pieters. “Even cells lacking coronins continue to organize and remodel their actin networks normally. Of course, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.”.

The team also identified a possible reason why earlier studies reached different conclusions. To observe proteins inside living cells, scientists often attach molecular tags that make them easier to track. Although these tools are widely used, they can sometimes interfere with the proteins being studied.

“These tags are extremely useful and assumed to be innocuous for protein function,” notes Roko Gvozdenica, the study’s first author. “However, we found that the tagging of coronin proteins has the potential to cause loss of their function and significantly alter their localization.”.

This raises the possibility that some earlier evidence linking coronins to actin resulted from experimental artifacts rather than their natural behavior. The researchers also found that many antibodies used to detect coronins lack specificity, adding to broader concerns about the reliability of these tools in biomedical research.

The findings bring attention to another important role of coronins: helping cells communicate through chemical signals.

“Over the years, we have reported that coronins are involved in cell signaling,” emphasizes Pieters. “In the immune system, for example, coronin involvement in these signaling processes was found to be essential for the maintenance of normal T cell numbers, which is vital for protecting the body against infections or cancer.”.

The researchers caution that their findings do not completely rule out a connection between coronins and the cytoskeleton. These proteins may still influence its organization, either directly or indirectly through cell signaling.

By reexamining an idea that has shaped research for decades, the study opens latest possibilities for understanding how coronins help cells communicate, survive, and maintain healthy cell numbers.

Reference: “Reassessment of the roles of coronin proteins as actin effectors and in signaling” by Roko Gvozdenica Šipić, Haiyan Zhang, Andrii Kharin, Jerneja Koren, Viviana D’Otolo, Yuko Nariai, Takeshi Urano, Pawel Pelczar, Klemens Fröhlich, Alexander Schmidt, Urszula Brykczynska Kunzmann, Tohnyui Ndinyanka Fabrice, Alexey Baldin and Jean Pieters, 18 August 2026, PLOS Biology. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003904.

Tech Report: Euclid's Hunt for Strong Gravitational Lenses is Off to a Strong Start

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness.
  • Luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns.
  • One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

Luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns. They're interesting problems for people who are intellectally curious about Nature. But for physicisits, the questions surrounding dark matter and dark energy are much more acute. Some of them dedicate their entire lives to understanding dark matter and dark energy. They design and build special telescopes, instruments, and spacecraft to make progress toward an answer.

One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.

This artist's illustration reveals the Euclid Space Telescope doing its thing in its halo orbit at L2. The telescope is on a six-year mission to create a 3D map of the sky, revealing how dark energy and dark matter shape the Universe. Image Credit: By ESA, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/128347141.

Dark matter and dark energy are foundational in our Universe. Dark matter doesn't interact with any light, but it's clearly there. It's some form of mass, but we don't know what. Dark matter is a placeholder term.

In a recent development, dark energy is another placeholder term. It describes the force driving the expansion of the Universe. Like dark matter, we can measure its effect, but we don't know what it really is. And the puzzling thing is that dark matter and dark energy make up most of the Universe.

âIt turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe,â said Dr. Douglas Scott, professor at the University of BC's department of physics and astronomy (PHAS) and member of the Euclid collaboration. âAnd what dominates â dark matter and dark energy â is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is, it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclidâs data gives us the potential to answer those questions.â.

This image reminds us that Euclid does more than study dark matter and dark energy. It's a powerful camera, after all, and can also capture stunning images of regular, baryonic matter, the kind that stars, people, and planets are made of. This image is from Euclid's Early Release Observations, and highlights the Messier 78 star formation region about 1300 light years away in Orion. This is the first time Messier 78 has been imaged with such width and depth, hallmarks of Euclid's observations. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi.

Industry observers note that euclid rolled out in July 2023 and orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), roughly 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth, a popular spot for space telescopes. From that perch, it uses its wide-angle, 600-megapixel camera to capture visible light, and a photometer and a near-infrared spectrometer to measure the redshift of about 10 billion sources out to redshift 2. That's roughly equivalent to about 10 billion years ago, or about 3.7 billion years after the Big Bang.

Among these sources, Euclid is especially interested in strong gravitational lenses. These are massive objects like galaxies, galaxy clusters, and dark matter halos. These objects can magnify background objects that are otherwise beyond observing. But they're critical for mapping dark matter itself, because their lensing effect is based on the total mass of these objects, not just their visible mass. So strong gravitational lenses are a way to measure the presence of dark matter. But they're not easy to find.

Sources indicate that euclid delivered its first data release on November 12th, called DR-1 Foundation, and it holds a whopping 1.7 million gigabytes of data. The data revealed almost 5% of the night sky in 13 months of observations. That data holds 900 million galaxies, and 60 million quasars, which are the extremely luminous cores of far-away galaxies. Euclid also found 15,000 newly introduced strong gravitational lens candidates, a massive increase in the potential number.

"Strong lenses have been difficult to find â the odds were about one in 10,000,â remarked Hrishabh Srivastava, doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). âBefore Euclid, we had less than a thousand confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 new candidates.â.

There's more than one type of gravitational lens. This is a collage of some of the different types of strong gravitational lenses Euclid has found so far. The top row indicates, from left to right: a classic galaxyâgalaxy lens, an Einstein ring in a face-on spiral lens, and an inclined dusty disc lens galaxy. The middle row shows an edge-on dusty lens galaxy, a lensed galaxy with visible star-forming regions, and a compound lens.The bottom row shows a galaxy group lens, a lensed quasar, and a galaxy group lens. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by N. Lines and T. Li. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence.

It has been revealed that overall, Euclid is expected to find more than 100,000 strong lenses over the course of its nominal six year mission. That would increase the number of known strong lenses by two orders of magnitude, a transformational advance for dark matter science.

âI like to call these gravitational lenses ânature's own magnifying glassesâ to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe,â stated Srivastava.

Industry observers note that strong gravitational lensing is an crucial tool, but so is weak gravitational lensing. They can be used together to build a fuller picture of dark matter and dark energy. The weak gravitational lensing signature is most apparent around massive galaxy clusters. Since weak gravitational lensing extends beyond a cluster's virial radius, it can help constrain a cluster's overall mass.

It has been revealed that finding huge numbers of gravitational lenses is clearly key in the quest to understand the Universe, but Euclid has other tasks, too. It will slowly build a 3D map of the Universe that covers greater than one-third of the sky. This map will comprise the actual tool used to measure dark matter and dark energy. The map will show how matter is distributed, and then that map can be tested against models of the Universe, especially Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Big Bang model of cosmology.

Lambda-CDM predicts how matter, including dark matter, is spread throughout the Universe, and how its structure is shaped by dark energy, which drives the Universe's expansion. So Euclid's 3D map can test both facets of Lambda-CDM: dark matter and dark energy. Dark energy is directly tested, and dark matter is tested more indirectly.

Euclid's test of Lambda-CDM won't be in one massive grand finale, where physicists around the world wait with bated breath to find out the answer. The test is ongoing. Each newly introduced data release will generate rounds of new research, as physicists and cosmologists dig into it. It'll be fuel for the different lines of detailed research that different teams of scientists pursue. It's like a process of elimination. Eventually, hopefully, the possible answers and explanations for dark matter and dark energy will be constrained and refined until only one is left standing.

Then, in all likelihood, Nobel prizes will be awarded.

But that won't be the end of cosmology. Latest questions will arise, intellectual curiosity will be piqued in new ways, and the quest to understand the Universe will continue.

But Euclid and its 3D map will be in history of science textbooks for a long time.

  • My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor.

It has been revealed that armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor.

Recent findings suggest that with a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

It has been revealed that I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

It has been revealed that every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

It has been revealed that with a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

It has been revealed that my Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Sources indicate that delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor.

Industry observers note that there’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Scientists Solve a Longstanding Mystery About the Tiny Gateways That Protect Our DNA

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protecting our DNA takes a surprisingly flexible defense, and scientists have uncovered how cells keep this microscopic barrier fluid rather than letting it harden.
  • Every minute, tens of thousands of molecules pass through tiny gateways in the membrane surrounding a cell’s nucleus, where its genetic material is stored.
  • “As the nuclear pore protects the genome and controls all exchange between the cell nucleus and the cytoplasm, it is one of the most important molecular machines in the human cell,” remarked Professor Miao Yu of Wuhan University in China, a co-first author of a upcoming study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protecting our DNA takes a surprisingly flexible defense, and scientists have uncovered how cells keep this microscopic barrier fluid rather than letting it harden.

Every minute, tens of thousands of molecules pass through tiny gateways in the membrane surrounding a cell’s nucleus, where its genetic material is stored. Known as nuclear pores, these openings allow certain molecules to enter or leave while blocking others. Scientists have long understood the structure of these gateways, yet the proteins controlling what gets through have remained a mystery. Do they form a rigid barrier, or something more like a constantly shifting liquid?

“As the nuclear pore protects the genome and controls all exchange between the cell nucleus and the cytoplasm, it is one of the most important molecular machines in the human cell,” remarked Professor Miao Yu of Wuhan University in China, a co-first author of a upcoming study published in Nature. “And also one of the most complex,” added co-first author Maziar Heidari of the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main, Germany.

Sources indicate that much of the uncertainty comes from how differently these proteins behave outside living cells. Previous experiments with isolated proteins produced everything from stretched chains to liquid-like droplets and thick gels resembling gummy bears. Some even formed solid deposits.

However, those observations could not establish what happens inside an actual nuclear pore, where thousands of molecular interactions help control traffic. “Such studies did not, however, allow any direct conclusions to be drawn about how the barrier behaves within the living cell,” mentioned Professor Edward Lemke, Professor of Synthetic Biophysics at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU).

To investigate the barrier in its natural environment, Lemke and his colleagues attached fluorescent dyes to proteins inside the nuclear pores of living cells. These tiny glowing markers allowed the researchers to track protein movement and determine how flexible the barrier remained. The proteins moved rapidly throughout the entire two-hour observation period, indicating that the interior of the pore behaves more like a fluid than a solid.

Industry observers note that “For the first time, we have been able to measure intrinsic protein dynamics within the nanocanal of a living cell and demonstrate that the interior of this canal is fluid-like,” mentioned Lemke, who led the study alongside Professor Gerhard Hummer of MPI-BP. “As the dyes move extremely quickly, the state inside the nuclear pores must be fluid-like,” he explained.

The contrast became clearer when the researchers compared their observations with proteins isolated in a test tube. After approximately two hours, the protein material consistently hardened into a gummy-bear-like gel or an even more rigid solid. Some of these deposits resembled protein accumulations associated with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Inside living cells, however, the barrier remained flexible over the same period. “This was a crucial turning point: there had to be something keeping the barrier in the cells dynamic,” remarked Lemke.

The researchers identified two components that helped explain the difference. One was a transport receptor, a protein involved in moving molecules through nuclear pores. The other was glycosylation, a process that attaches sugar groups to proteins and helps prevent them from sticking together too tightly. When both were included in the laboratory model, the proteins regained much of the mobility observed in living cells. “When we add these two components, we observe a similar mobility in the model system to that found in the nuclear pores of living cells,” said Lemke.

According to recent reports, understanding the barrier’s flexibility also helped the team tackle another longstanding puzzle: where molecules actually travel as they pass through the pore. In an ordinary pipe or river, flow is generally fastest near the center and slower along the edges. Earlier research suggested that nuclear pores work differently, with much of the transport occurring near their outer walls. One proposed explanation was that a biological structure, possibly a plug, occupied the middle and forced molecules toward the sides.

Recent findings suggest that hummer’s team investigated this possibility using what the researchers describe as the most comprehensive simulation model of a nuclear pore developed to date. The model incorporated experimental measurements from the Mainz team, including how extensively the barrier proteins were linked to one another. It allowed the researchers to examine how molecules would move through a pore with the physical properties they had measured.

“The simulations confirm that the main transport route runs along the edge of the pore,” remarked Hummer. Importantly, the calculations showed that this pattern could emerge from the pore’s physical and chemical properties without requiring a central obstruction. “While we do not rule out a biological cause such as a plug, it is not necessary from a physicochemical point of view.”.

It has been revealed that producing such a detailed model required enormous computing power. “These complex calculations were made possible by JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale supercomputer at the Jülich Research Center,” said Hummer.

The experiments and simulations provide a clearer picture of how nuclear pores maintain a flexible barrier while regulating the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus. They may also help researchers investigate why proteins that normally remain flexible sometimes harden into deposits, a process involved in neurodegenerative diseases.

Reference: “Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores” by Miao Yu (于淼), Maziar Heidari, Karen Palacio-Rodriguez, Hao Ruan (阮浩), Sara Mingu, Yu Chen (陈宇), Xu-Zhuo Gou (缑绪卓), Pingkai Shen (沈平恺), Songzi Liu (刘松子), Si-Yu Chen (陈思宇), Alam Ahmad Hidayat, Mathis Bode, Mateusz Sikora, Ai-Hui Tang (唐爱辉), Gerhard Hummer and Edward A. Lemke, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11258-0.
